Can your token draw?

Technically, yes, it can. The JS code is using a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) model, which was trained on human hand drawings. The model was created and trained by The Magenta Team. The RNN model tries to predict the next point of the sketch, when a previous point is given.

The token comes with a 'Type' and 'Color' feature, the type will determine what your token can draw. Possibilities are: Cat, Bird, Tractor, Skull, Ambulance and Pig. Each type has a different rarity.

The model first must be initialized, so you have to wait couple of seconds until it gets start drawing. Every time you refresh the token, it will draw a different sketch from the same type.

Enjoy!
Bálint Kulcsár, 2021

A Pico-8 simulation of the Three Body Problem. This is a rework of the initial generative project that got me started as an artist (and my earliest series on HEN). This is a live simulation, coded and running entirely on the Pico-8, of the Three Body Problem: a famous example of a chaotic system that cannot be predicted. The mass of all three bodies in this simulation are identical.

Uses features to track most variables. Initial position and velocity of all three bodies are randomly determined according to the fxhash. As well, collisions are disabled for the first three seconds of the simulation, in order to increase the variety of the outcomes.

If viewing the piece in its own browser window, press ctrl+9 to save a 16 second gif (of the last 16 seconds of the simulation), press ctrl+6 to save a png.

Tap to start sound. Tap to mute.

Inspired by the glass rondelles which hung from the windowsill in my childhood home. I ask myself what would these rondelles sound like if they reflected sound instead of light? To me, I hear hopeful harmonies of memories past, but they are falling in and out of tune and they are occluded by the muffled noise of time.

When a rondelle is minted, a transaction hash is injected into its code. All colors, patterns, sounds, and motions are generated deterministically from this transaction hash.

As the rondelle loads in your browser, a real-time generative algorithm writes tones, noise, feedback, and distortion to three looping audio buffers. During playback, oscillations in pan, pitch, and volume track the visual oscillations among the rondelle's color rings.

Rarity features are included. The least common rondelles are closed center, monochrome, smol, split color, and square.

Made with Web Audio and p5js. Minted on fxhash beta. Idlebit, 2021.

830.d:
Generator of virtually infinite drawings based on epicyclic motions. 
 
A polyline of three or more segments rotates around a predefined center, progressively changing its configuration. The center of rotation is located at the top outside the display area. The changes are made by rotating the first segment around the center and subsequent segments around the end vertex of the previous one. The segments from the second onward are drawn at each frame, and all traces are then moved down.

Depending on the lengths of the segments and the individual rotation speeds, the drawings can repeat in the same exact way after a few minutes or after very many years.
 
Antonio Belluscio (@livinbits)
November 2021

Viewing in live mode on smartphones or in portrait format windows is recommended.
With a click or tap, you can increase/decrease the scrolling speed.

Pegs In Motion adds a twist to the original PEGS project by adding animation, rotating the pegs to make the string loop around the grid and bring the artwork alive. Forever limited to 500 unique editions on the Tezos blockchain.

Taking inspiration from work by Karl Gerstner, Armin Hofmann, Nick Kuder and Dmitri Cherniak, Pegs In Motion explores the limits of constrained algorithmic variation. Based on the simple, playful idea of wrapping a string across a board of pegs, it shows how endless possibilities can be achieved with just a basic set of rules and a few primary colors. When done right, generative art challenges us to answer fundamental questions around creativity, beauty, and life itself.

859.d:
The third of four operations, this further extrapolates the algorithm. Per-view randomization is in the speed and size of the drawing of the rays, and in the placement of the Voronoi points. Each viewing is unique, but each mint is also unique.

The image draws in its entirety in about 10 seconds. After 20 seconds, it clears, randomizes the placement, and draws again. Full-screen capable.

Three traits describe each individual mint:

Color: There are nine different color palettes, with "Leaves" being a 20% likelihood, and all the others 10% likelihood.

Arc: This is the number of elements drawn around each point. There are three possible states, with 50 being a 10% likelihood, 250 being a 20% likelihood, and 100 being the default at 70%.

Resolution: This is the number of points in the Voronoi field. There are four candidates, with 1 being the least likely (10%), 2 and 3 having a 20% likelihood of occurring, and 4 being the most common at 50%.

Created in p5.js

863.d:
Re-appropriating Andy Warhol's "Marilyn Monroe, 1967," (originally appropriated from Eugene Kornmann's photo of the actress) as a generative art piece. 

How will we look back upon our Icons? 
Once we pick them apart, can we ever put them back together again?

Technical notes:
There are no image files contained within the package: the script places random shapes by looking up the coordinates and colors in an included text file. A random "Chaos" value is introduced, and then compounded by a growing "Entropy" value. The final result is a completely unique 36" x 36" artwork. Some will be so uniform in pattern that they are instantly recognizable as expressions of the inspirational work. Most will be a gradient of sorts, from order to chaos. A rare few will be completely transformed by disorder.

There are 25 named color palettes for these 32 editions.

868.d:
Binary neighbourliness based on a simple rule where if a block has the same binary value as its 3 neighbours they become friends.

How this works under the hood:
1. Hash determines grid size
2. Hash is also converted into an array of numbers from chunking the hashes.
3. Hash is converted to binary and a subset of the binary string is chosen according to a hashed numeric value based on the grid size
4. If a block has the same binary value as its 3 neighbours they all take on the same properties and turn red.

The ⓂⒺⓉⒶⒷⓄⓁⒾⓈⓂ series is a tribute to japanese industrial design from the post-war industrialization of the country. Architects of the era, -- known as the 'Metabolists'-- imagined structures made of modular blocks like the unfamous Nagakin tower in Tokyo. This series is inspired by architectural sketches of the time and the work of Japanese graphic designers from the 60s / 70s such as Yusaku Kamekura, recognizable by his concentric shapes.

905.d:
Square Spiral Tile’o’rama
(2021)
By Clockwork Feathers

There are three main components to this image generator. The first is the square spiral tile generation algorithm, which is a routine based off of cellular automata algorithms, but instead of having it iterate in the second dimension, the routine simulates the second dimension in computed offsets in a one dimensional array. That array then gets rolled up into a square “tile.”

The second component is a probability based tiling routine that takes in a generated tile routine and then fills in a specified percentage of the larger image with randomly rotated input tiles. This routine is called repeatedly with adjusted probabilities for smaller tiles. 

Finally, there is a collection of color pallet generation functions. There are eight formulas for choosing a color pallet for the generated image, and one is chosen at random for each run.

For more info on me and my creative practice, find me on Instagram @clockworkfeathers and on twitter @ClkworkFeathers

981.d:
De/Frag is an homage to a classic algorithm in early computer art: Flood Fill. As a teenager in the late '80s, and without any literature, I spent weeks implementing a version for my very own drawing program for the Atari XL. It was the first non-trivial (to me) algorithm which made me want to learn more about data structures, the concept of recursion, divide-and-conquer...

Even though Flood Fill was available in most commercial drawing & office apps of the time, I gained a deep appreciation of the algorithm by building it from scratch myself. 30+ years later I know its aesthetic possibilities are still far from exhausted. This is an invitation for re-exploration by others too!

As with many design algorithms, my primary interest isn't even the final result, but observing the inner workings. I massively slowed down and time-sliced the process for this piece. I do recommend giving each of these unique versions some time to allow them to evolve their ever-changing patterns (Note: each piece never loops!).

983.d: The story of a kid who has a strange encounter with an alien spacecraft. The kid, played by Joey Cramer, does a solid job playing a lead role. He talks and acts like a kid would without being cute. Maybe this movie will be the end of the live-action child character curse. The spaceship, named Max and voiced by Paul Reubens (Pee Wee Herman), and the kid have an interesting dynamic. As the story progressed, I would have liked to see more development of their relationship. I remember loving this movie as a kid, but now that I’m older I see that, as a kid, I was the target demographic for this movie. There are a few things to like as an adult, but not enough to really recommend a repeat viewing. One view should be enough.
